title: P-Sh-T

cards: Two eggs. That's the whole line on an old recipe card, in faded ink. A clever cook could read deep things into it, about pairs, about beginnings, about fragile shells.
The cake doesn't care. The card means two eggs. Jewish reading has a name for what a text simply says, before anyone gets clever: peshat, the plain sense.
In modern Hebrew the same root gives pashut, simple, obvious. Pey, shin, tet: P-Sh-T. Yesterday the rabbis dug.
Today they make sure the ground is still there.

teach.h: THE CLOTH: NOTHING LAID OVER IT.
teach.b: Turn this root four ways. First, the cloth. In the Bible's Hebrew, the verb from this root has to do with spreading out and stripping off.
When Joseph's brothers take his coat from him, the verb is this one. Peshat is a text with nothing laid over it, in plain view. Second, the anchor.

The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, sets down a short rule: a verse does not leave its plain meaning. Midrash can soar, but it can't cut the rope. Even the boldest reading has to come home to the words on the page.

teach.h: THE ANCHOR: A VERSE KEEPS ITS PLAIN SENSE.
teach.b: Rashi, a medieval commentator you've sat beside since day one hundred fifty-three, says on a verse in Genesis that he has come only for the plain sense, and for those teachings that help the words make sense.

teach.h: THE FLOOR: EVERYTHING STANDS ON IT.
teach.b: Later Jewish teachers described levels of reading, as you saw on day eight hundred eighty-five, and peshat is the floor everything else stands on. Above it come hints, seeking and secrets.
But nobody climbs without a floor. Look back over the week: creating and forming, wisdom and command, walking, seeking, and now the plain.
Six days of digging into words, and the seventh says: before you dig, read what's there.

how: Jewish students traditionally learn the Torah with Rashi's commentary, which aims at the plain sense, and Jewish tradition holds that a verse never departs from its peshat even when it is also read through midrash.

games.q: you're reading a verse with a clever new interpretation in mind. what does the rule in tractate Shabbat say?
o: the clever reading replaces the plain one.
the verse still keeps its plain meaning.
only the plain reading is allowed.
games.why: a verse does not leave its plain meaning. midrash can add, but it can't cut the rope.

practice: Here is a verse from the first chapter of Genesis: "And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light."

Say it slowly and resist every urge to explain it, no symbolism, no theory, no lesson, just what it says: someone spoke, light was. Notice what the plain words do on their own, and then let yourself rest with them.

wordCard.voice: P-Sh-T. Pey, shin, tet: the root of peshat, the plain sense of a text, and of pashut, simple. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the plain sense of a text; related to pashut, simple.

carryVoice: Your line: plain. On a recipe card, two eggs means two eggs. Fourteen hundred days now, one plain step at a time.
